Jacques Demy. A French New Wave director whose romantic, musically inclined sensibility set him apart from his contemporaries. He created luminous, colour-saturated films that married French realism with American musical tradition, yielding melancholic love stories and dreamlike fables. His films radiate an emotional sincerity unusual among the New Wave's self-conscious formalists.

He directed The Umbrellas of Cherbourg in 1964, a breakthrough musical romance filmed entirely in saturated primary colours, about a young woman and her sailor lover separated by circumstance. He made Lola in 1961, exploring the overlapping love lives of a French prostitute and various men in her orbit—a predecessor to the episodic, romance-centred narratives of his mature work.

Demy composed his films with Michel Legrand, creating delicate, jazz-inflected scores that humanise moments of romantic loss and longing. He cast Catherine Deneuve, Anouk Aimée, and other actresses as the romantic centres of his narratives, inhabiting their interiority and yearning. He bridged the New Wave's formal innovation with popular musical cinema, proving that avant-garde technique could serve emotional accessibility.

His visual world is one of pastel colours and geometric precision, with frames as carefully composed as paintings. Later work grew darker, exploring crime and moral ambiguity, though never abandoning lyricism. He shares with François Truffaut the role of fellow New Wave humanist—both prioritised feeling over formalism. He rejected the formalism and political austerity of Jean-Luc Godard. Michel Legrand was his composer and frequent collaborator, their partnership defining Demy's signature sound. Catherine Deneuve was his muse and actor, her face embodying Demy's romantic vision.
